mainTopic: Whether liquid that seeps out of fruit without the owner wanting it still counts as a 'liquid' (משקה), and whether the רבנן agree with רבי יהודה about fruits other than olives and grapes
overview: This amud opens in the middle of a quoted משנה in which רבי עקיבא and the חכמים argue about animal milk that comes out without the owner wanting it. The חכמים say an animal's fluids are more lenient, since its wound-blood is טהור. רבי עקיבא answers that milk is stricter than blood. The חכמים then bring baskets of olives and grapes as proof that liquid coming out unwanted does not count. The גמרא tries to use that rule in a קל וחומר: unwanted juice from mulberries and pomegranates should surely not count either. It rejects the proof in two ways. Either 'unwillingly' means the owner openly objected, or the baskets are a special case because the dripping liquid is given up from the start. Finally, the גמרא asks for a source that the רבנן agree with רבי יהודה about other fruits, and it begins quoting a ברייתא that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The חכמים finish rejecting רבי עקיבא's comparison of animal milk to human milk
steps.stepSummary: The end of the חכמים' rebuttal: human milk can be different, because her wound-blood is טמא, while an animal's wound-blood is טהור.
steps.simpleTranslation: [Will animal milk that came out] unwillingly [count], when the blood of its wound is pure?!
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the middle of a quoted משנה. The חכמים are finishing their answer to רבי עקיבא's קל וחומר from human milk to animal milk.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי עקיבא argued that animal milk should count as a liquid even when it comes out unwanted, just like human milk. The חכמים reply that the comparison fails. With a woman, even blood from a wound counts as a liquid. With an animal, blood from a wound does not count (it is טהור). So the animal's fluids are treated more leniently.

keyTerms.meaning: not willingly; without the owner wanting it
pure; here, it does not make food able to become impure

steps.confusionAlert: Here 'טהור' does not mean the blood itself is clean. It means this fluid does not count as one of the liquids that make food able to receive טומאה (הכשר).

phrases.english: [that came out] unwillingly,
phrases.notes: Continues from the previous daf: 'shall animal milk be impure when it comes out...'

phrases.english: when the blood of its wound is pure?!
phrases.notes: Rhetorical: the animal's fluids are treated more leniently.

steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבי עקיבא's קל וחומר from human milk to animal milk
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Human milk is stricter because even her wound-blood counts as a liquid, while an animal's wound-blood does not.

steps.title: רבי עקיבא explains why milk is stricter than blood
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא answers that milk is treated more strictly than blood, so the leniency of blood proves nothing about milk.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I am stricter with milk than with blood. Someone who milks an animal for medical reasons, the milk is טמא (it counts). Someone who lets blood for medical reasons, the blood is טהור (it does not count).
steps.whatsHappening: רבי עקיבא defends his קל וחומר. He says you cannot learn milk from blood, because milk is a stronger liquid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Milk taken only for medical reasons, not for drinking, still counts as a liquid. Blood let for medical reasons does not count. Since milk counts even when blood does not, the fact that an animal's wound-blood is טהור tells us nothing about its milk.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶן: מַחְמִיר אֲנִי בֶּחָלָב מִבַּדָּם,
phrases.english: He [Rabbi Akiva] said to them: I am stricter with milk than with blood,
for one who milks for medical purposes, [the milk] is impure [it counts as a liquid],
while one who lets blood for medical purposes, [the blood] is pure [it does not count].

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לָהֶן: מַחְמִיר אֲנִי בֶּחָלָב מִבַּדָּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the חכמים' rebuttal in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinction: milk is a stronger liquid than blood
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since an animal's blood is lenient, its milk should be lenient too.
steps.terutzMaskana: Milk counts even in cases where blood does not, so blood is no model for milk.

steps.title: The חכמים bring olive and grape baskets as proof that willingness matters
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים prove from olive and grape baskets that a real liquid still does not count when it comes out without the owner wanting it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: Baskets of olives and grapes will prove it. Liquid that comes out of them willingly is טמא (it counts). Liquid that comes out unwillingly is טהור (it does not count).
steps.whatsHappening: The חכמים answer רבי עקיבא with a counter-proof. Even strong liquids like oil and wine do not count if they came out against the owner's will.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Oil and wine are definitely real liquids, yet liquid that seeps from the baskets without the owner wanting it does not count. So being a 'strong' liquid is not enough. The owner's will decides, and animal milk that comes out unwanted can also be טהור.
steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's rule is that liquid seeping from olive and grape baskets counts only when it came out לרצון.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: סַלֵּי זֵיתִים וַעֲנָבִים יוֹכִיחוּ,
phrases.english: They said to him: baskets of olives and grapes will prove it,
for the liquids that come out of them willingly are impure [they count],
[but those that come out] unwillingly are pure [they do not count].

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרוּ לוֹ: סַלֵּי זֵיתִים וַעֲנָבִים יוֹכִיחוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Counters רבי עקיבא's answer in step 2.
steps.raayaObject: That the owner's will, not the strength of the liquid, decides whether it counts
steps.raayaSupportSource: The case of liquid seeping from baskets of olives and grapes

steps.title: The גמרא tries to learn about mulberries and pomegranates from this משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reads 'לרצון' as 'actually wanted' and 'שלא לרצון' as 'no opinion'. It then argues by קל וחומר that unwanted juice from mulberries and pomegranates surely does not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: Doesn't 'willingly' mean he was pleased, and 'unwillingly' mean he had no opinion either way? If olives and grapes, which are meant for squeezing, have liquid that counts for nothing when it comes out without his will, then mulberries and pomegranates, which are not meant for squeezing, all the more so!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now uses the quoted משנה for its own question about juice that seeps from mulberries and pomegranates. It is trying to prove that such juice does not count as a liquid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key move is how the words are defined. If 'שלא לרצון' covers even a case where the owner simply had no opinion, then unwanted seepage from olives and grapes does not count. Those fruits are usually squeezed, so their liquid is important. Mulberries and pomegranates are usually eaten, so their seepage should surely be ignored (a קל וחומר).

keyTerms.meaning: isn't it true that...? (introduces a proposed proof)
in an unspecified case; he had no opinion
isn't it all the more so?

phrases.english: Is it not that 'willingly' means that he is pleased with it,
and 'unwillingly' means an unspecified case [he had no opinion]?
And if olives and grapes,
which are meant for squeezing,
[when liquid comes out] unwillingly, it is nothing,
then mulberries and pomegranates,
which are not meant for squeezing,
is it not all the more so?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the חכמים' rule from step 3 and applies it to the גמרא's own question.
steps.raayaObject: That juice seeping without intent from mulberries and pomegranates does not count as a liquid
steps.raayaSupportSource: The olive and grape basket rule in the משנה, plus a קל וחומר

steps.title: Rejection: 'unwillingly' means he said explicitly that he does not want it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof by redefining the terms. 'לרצון' includes a case with no opinion, and 'שלא לרצון' means he openly said he does not want it.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. 'Willingly' means even when he had no opinion. 'Unwillingly' means he showed what he thinks and said: 'I am not pleased with it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 4 by reading the words of the משנה differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'שלא לרצון' only covers an owner who openly objected, then the משנה says nothing about a case with no opinion. In fact, under this reading, a case with no opinion counts as 'לרצון', and the liquid does count. So the קל וחומר about mulberries and pomegranates falls apart.

keyTerms.meaning: I am not pleased with it

steps.confusionAlert: The same words 'לרצון / שלא לרצון' are read in two opposite ways. In step 4 the 'no opinion' case is called unwilling. In step 5 the 'no opinion' case is called willing. Keep track of where the 'no opinion' case lands.

phrases.english: No: 'willingly' [includes] an unspecified case,
and 'unwillingly' means he revealed his intention,
saying: 'I am not pleased with it.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the definition of the terms used in step 4.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proof from the משנה about the 'no opinion' case
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It assumed 'שלא לרצון' includes a case with no opinion. It may mean only an openly stated objection.

steps.title: Second rejection: liquid seeping from baskets is given up from the start
steps.stepSummary: Even if 'שלא לרצון' means 'no opinion', olive and grape baskets are a special case, because the owner gives up in advance on liquid that drips out and gets lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you could say: baskets of olives and grapes are different. Since that liquid is going to be lost anyway, he declares it ownerless from the start.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second, independent way to reject the proof from step 4.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer keeps step 4's definitions but limits the case. The dripping from a basket is expected to be lost, so the owner gives it up ahead of time, and that is why it does not count. Juice from fruits that is not expected to be lost could still count even without stated approval, so nothing can be learned about mulberries and pomegranates.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you want, say instead (an alternative answer)
it is going to be lost
he completely gives it up as ownerless

steps.whatToRemember: Both rejections leave the question about unwanted juice from mulberries and pomegranates without a proof from the משנה.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: שָׁאנֵי סַלֵּי זֵיתִים וַעֲנָבִים,
phrases.english: And if you wish, say: baskets of olives and grapes are different,
since [their seeping liquid] is going to be lost,
from the start he gives it up as ownerless.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא: שָׁאנֵי סַלֵּי זֵיתִים וַעֲנָבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second rejection of step 4, independent of step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Applying the basket case to fruits in general
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The basket case is special: the owner gives up the liquid in advance because it will be lost.

steps.title: Source needed that the רבנן agree with רבי יהודה about other fruits
steps.stepSummary: We already know רבי יהודה agrees with the רבנן about olives and grapes. The גמרא asks for a source that the רבנן agree with רבי יהודה about other fruits.
steps.simpleTranslation: We found that רבי יהודה agrees with the רבנן about olives and grapes. From where do we know that the רבנן agree with רבי יהודה about other fruits?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new question and asks for a source. The next step begins to answer it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An earlier ברייתא showed that רבי יהודה agrees with the רבנן that juice seeping from olives and grapes on שבת is forbidden. Now the גמרא wants the reverse. It asks whether the רבנן accept רבי יהודה's distinction for other fruits: fruits meant for eating are permitted, and fruits meant for juice are forbidden.

phrases.english: We have found that Rabbi Yehuda agrees with the Rabbis
regarding olives and grapes.
That the Rabbis agree with Rabbi Yehuda
regarding other fruits, from where do we know it?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַשְׁכְּחַן רַבִּי יְהוּדָה דְּמוֹדֵי לְרַבָּנַן בְּזֵיתִים וּבַעֲנָבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the mulberry discussion and returns to the larger argument between רבי יהודה and the רבנן.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A source that the רבנן accept רבי יהודה's distinction for fruits other than olives and grapes

steps.title: The גמרא begins quoting a ברייתא as the source
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא starts bringing a ברייתא ('One may squeeze...') to answer the question. The text continues on the next amud.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it was taught in a ברייתא: One may squeeze...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is opening its proof for step 7. The ברייתא's content continues in the next section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'דתניא' signals that a ברייתא will be quoted as the answer. Its first word, 'סוחטין' (one may squeeze), hints that the ברייתא will allow squeezing certain fruits on שבת. That would show that the רבנן also treat fruits not meant for juice more leniently.

keyTerms.meaning: as it was taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: As it was taught [in a baraita]: One may squeeze...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins answering the question of step 7.
steps.raayaObject: That the רבנן agree with רבי יהודה about other fruits
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא beginning 'סוחטין' (continued on the next amud)
